title: Topologically protected quantum matter outside the dilution refrigerator

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a solid-state material that supports verified non-Abelian quasiparticles and protected quantum operations at liquid-nitrogen temperature or above. These quasiparticles are collective excitations of the material. Their fusion—combining them and measuring the outcome—or braiding—exchanging their positions—could encode and manipulate quantum information. The material would need a verified topological energy gap and evidence that its operations possess the protection attributed to that quantum phase. The supplied experimental record establishes a cryogenic readout capability, while the high-temperature material and operations remain a target.

Scope synthesis: the advance concerns creating and verifying the requisite quantum phase in a material, together with demonstrating operations that use it. A suggestive transport signature, a fermion-parity measurement, or a material described as topological would not by itself establish this capability. The proposed temperature boundary is nitrogen’s boiling temperature at standard atmospheric pressure; it does not require room-temperature operation. Manufacturability would be a further practical achievement.

significance.text: Non-Abelian anyons offer a route to quantum operations whose behavior depends on collective topological properties. The technical motivation described in the reviewed research is exponential suppression of errors induced by local noise during protected fusion and braiding operations. Demonstrating such operations at liquid-nitrogen temperature or above would make this quantum-information platform substantially more thermally accessible than the documented InAs–Al devices operated in dilution refrigerators.

The direct consequence would be a materials platform for protected non-Abelian operations outside the dilution refrigerator. Conditionally, reproducible fabrication and scalable control could make that platform useful for quantum information processing. Protection against local noise does not imply immunity to every error: the reviewed technical account describes a discrete set of native topological operations and retains a role for error-correction schemes. Useful computation would still require readout, wiring, control, scale and error management.

Impact synthesis: removing the dilution-refrigerator requirement for the active material would not automatically remove cooling requirements elsewhere in a system, establish economical manufacturing, or demonstrate a useful quantum computer. Nor would success by this criterion establish ambient dissipationless spin transport or axion-insulator memory. Those would require their own physical and device demonstrations; their connection to the proposed non-Abelian capability is undocumented in the supplied evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is the combined demonstration of a protective topological gap, non-Abelian quasiparticles, and fusion or braiding at the proposed elevated temperature. In the documented InAs–Al platform, the central identification barrier is that fine-tuned low-energy Andreev bound states in a topologically trivial phase can produce a competing interpretation of the parity-readout signal. The original authors acknowledge that their measurements alone do not determine whether the detected low-energy states are topological. Establishing readout therefore leaves a separate scientific task: identifying the states and demonstrating their non-Abelian behavior.

The protective gap is itself part of the unresolved experimental interpretation. Legg’s 2026 criticism challenges the transport-based gap identification and argues that an absence of a robust superconducting gap would undermine the interpretation. Microsoft’s reply argues that a gapless system would lose the stable interferometric signal. Resolving this disagreement requires evidence that distinguishes the physical mechanisms, rather than treating either parity readout or the critique alone as conclusive.

Engineering synthesis: an elevated-temperature implementation must maintain the relevant quantum phase and an effective protective gap under the thermal conditions of operation, while allowing quasiparticle preparation, control and readout. It must also show that thermal excitations and device imperfections do not erase the claimed protection over useful operating times. The supplied sources document a cryogenic superconducting hybrid; they do not establish a route to this higher-temperature regime or a field-wide inventory of alternative platforms.

current_state.text: Microsoft Azure Quantum reported single-shot interferometric measurement of fermion parity in indium arsenide–aluminium heterostructures with a gate-defined superconducting nanowire, in Nature 638, 651–655, published online on 19 February 2025. The reported platform operates at an approximately 2 T magnetic field. This is a demonstrated readout capability. The article presents the architecture as compatible with future fusion-rule tests; the accompanying editorial statement likewise distinguishes the published architecture from future fusion experiments using Majorana zero modes.

The article’s main-text introduction states that the measurement alone cannot unequivocally distinguish Majorana zero modes in a topological phase from fine-tuned low-energy Andreev bound states in a trivial phase. Its discussion similarly limits what the interferometry establishes about the low-energy states. Thus the reported parity measurement does not, by itself, demonstrate topological quasiparticles, non-Abelian fusion or braiding, or protected quantum operations.

The temperature evidence includes two distinct uses of 50 mK. Figure 4 uses T = 50 mK as a simulation parameter. Separately, supplementary Section S10 reports an inferred electron temperature of 50 ± 13 mK at refrigerator base temperature for device-B thermometry. Supplementary Section S5 also describes device-B measurements in a different dilution refrigerator with the same wiring configuration. These observations establish cryogenic operation within their stated scope; the thermometry should not be assigned indiscriminately to every experimental trace. The supplied review had access to these supplementary sections, although the extracted supplement was truncated later in its references.

Legg’s Matters Arising, Nature 654, E22–E26, published on 24 June 2026, challenges the transport-based identification of the gap. Its accessible opening argues that an absence of a robust superconducting gap would contradict a prerequisite of the interpretation and would suggest a trivial origin for the signals. That is a qualified criticism, not an established finding that the signals are trivial. Microsoft Quantum’s published reply defends the parity-readout interpretation, arguing that a gapless system would wash out the stable h/2e-periodic bimodal interferometric signal through loss of oscillation amplitude or the relevant time scales.

The supplied review could access only subscription previews of the complete published 2026 comment and reply. An available peer-review file contains contrasting reviewer judgments and author rebuttals, including a reviewer’s assessment that the critique did not provide a definitive alternative explanation. This documents disagreement without resolving the physical origin of the signals. The review also did not inspect the figure images, limiting its ability to adjudicate arguments that depend on those images. These access limits do not establish that either interpretation is false.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record does not establish a qualifying elevated-temperature material, but it also does not substantiate a field-wide claim that none exists. Its freshness record is empty, so the broader state of the field as of 1 November 2026 remains unverified. The defensible conclusion is that the documented InAs–Al result is cryogenic and its topological interpretation remains contested.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: two independent groups, using separately fabricated material, would verify a protective topological gap and demonstrate the same non-Abelian fusion or braiding rule at or above nitrogen’s boiling temperature at standard atmospheric pressure. Each result would need to connect the observed rule to the claimed quasiparticles and quantum phase. Independent replication, separate fabrication and this temperature threshold are proposed criteria for this record, not established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independently replicated gap and non-Abelian rule at nitrogen’s boiling temperature or above

completion_criteria.text: Proposed discrimination and protection tests: pre-registered measurements would distinguish the claimed non-Abelian behavior from specified trivial-Andreev alternatives and test the robustness attributed to topological protection. Gap evidence, state identification and operational evidence should be assessed together, because the reviewed experiment explicitly leaves the topological identity of its detected states unresolved. The rationale follows from the documented ambiguity; the proposed measurement requirements go beyond the demonstrated readout architecture.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-registered tests distinguish non-Abelian behavior and assess topological protection

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: reports would specify measured temperature, magnetic field, device geometry, fabrication variation, operating times, error behavior and the tested perturbation range. Replication would establish demonstrated breadth across those conditions, rather than literal universality or protection against every possible disturbance. A millikelvin parity-readout result in an aluminium-proximitized nanowire would remain below the proposed temperature threshold even if its topological interpretation were accepted. Claims of manufacturability or useful computing would require additional evidence of fabrication yield, scalable control and system performance.
completion_criteria.label: Reports specify operating conditions, error behavior and demonstrated replication breadth

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison—MAS-01, Ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductivity in a manufacturable solid: both concepts seek quantum-material capabilities under more accessible thermal conditions. Superconductivity is relevant to the documented InAs–Al hybrid, but superconductivity alone would not demonstrate a topological gap, non-Abelian quasiparticles or protected fusion and braiding. Conversely, MAS-10’s proposed nitrogen-temperature threshold does not establish MAS-01’s room-temperature, ambient-pressure and manufacturing requirements. They remain distinct innovations.

Roster synthesis—MAS-03, General atomically precise covalent construction, and MAS-04, A reliable map from a property specification to a makeable material: precise construction and reliable material design could help develop or reproduce a suitable quantum material. Their targets are general construction and design capabilities, whereas MAS-10 requires a particular quantum phase and verified operations. Success in any one would not establish the others.

Roster synthesis—the remaining entries address different material functions: MAS-02 concerns strength and damage tolerance; MAS-05 concerns structural survival under fusion-level atomic displacement; MAS-06 concerns reversible energy storage at chemical-fuel specific energy; MAS-07 concerns programmable growth of load-bearing solids; MAS-08 concerns ambient nitrogen fixation at industrial intensity; and MAS-09 concerns recovery of structural metals from macroscopic fracture in service. The supplied evidence establishes no specific dependency between these capabilities and protected non-Abelian operations. Their distinct completion requirements should remain separate.

unresolved_issues: The physical origin and topological character of the documented InAs–Al signals remain unresolved in the supplied evidence.
The complete published 2026 comment and reply were unavailable to the supplied review; figure images were not inspected.
Field-wide availability of qualifying elevated-temperature materials remains unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The supplied evidence does not establish a material route to elevated-temperature protected non-Abelian operations or quantitative gap and robustness targets for such a route.
Specific pre-registered measurements, alternative-mechanism models and acceptable operational error bounds remain to be defined; the proposed completion criteria are not established standards.
Manufacturability, scalable control and useful computation require demonstrations beyond the proposed material-and-operation milestone.

brief.title: Protected quantum operations with less cooling
possible: Researchers could store and manipulate quantum information in a solid cooled with liquid nitrogen, or operating warmer. The material would protect operations from local disturbances, without needing the extreme cold of a dilution refrigerator.

The operations would combine or exchange quasiparticles: collective excitations within a material that behave like particles. Their verified behavior, together with an energy gap that shields the quantum state, would provide the protection.
why: Quantum computing researchers would gain a platform that sharply suppresses errors from local noise at much more accessible temperatures. This would expand the materials and operating conditions available for protected quantum information processing.

sources.showed: They read fermion parity, whether an electron count is odd or even, in a single measurement of an indium arsenide–aluminium device. The readout had an assignment error probability of 1%.
sources.quote: The large capacitance shift and long poisoning time enable a parity measurement with an assignment error probability of 1%.
sources.cited_for: The experiment establishes a readout capability needed for protected quantum operations.
sources.not_established: The measurement does not identify protected quasiparticles or demonstrate their operations at liquid-nitrogen temperature.

sources.showed: His analysis of electrical transport data found that the readout regions appeared to lack an energy gap. He argued that this challenged the proposed physical explanation.
sources.quote: this analysis reveals that the claimed parity readout occurred in regions of phase space with considerable disorder that appear gapless.
sources.cited_for: The protective energy gap remains disputed.
sources.not_established: The critique does not conclusively establish an alternative physical origin for the signals.

sources.showed: They argued that a system without an energy gap would lose the stable interference signal they observed, defending their interpretation against Legg’s critique.
sources.cited_for: The researchers dispute the claim that their readout came from a system without an energy gap.
sources.not_established: The reply does not demonstrate protected operations or settle the physical identity of the measured states.

shown: Microsoft Azure Quantum has demonstrated parity readout in devices operated in an extremely cold refrigerator. The authors acknowledge that the measurement alone cannot distinguish the desired quantum states from ordinary states that mimic them.
missing: A material must sustain the protective energy gap and the required quasiparticles at liquid-nitrogen temperature or above.
Combining or exchanging those quasiparticles must demonstrate the claimed quantum rules and protection from disturbances.
Preparation, control and readout must work while heat and device imperfections leave the protection intact over useful operating times.

milestones.label: Independent replication at liquid-nitrogen temperature or above
milestones.explanation: Two independent groups using separately made materials would verify a protective gap and the same non-Abelian rule, a distinctive combining or exchange behavior, at nitrogen’s standard-pressure boiling point or above. This would establish repeatability.

milestones.label: Tests distinguish the quantum behavior and demonstrate protection
milestones.explanation: Tests specified in advance would distinguish the claimed behavior from ordinary lookalike states and measure its resistance to disturbances. This would link the gap, the states and the operations to the claimed protection.

milestones.label: Operating limits and replication breadth are measured
milestones.explanation: Reports would give temperature, magnetic field, geometry, fabrication variation, operating times, errors and tested disturbances across replications. This would establish the conditions over which the protection works.

uncertain: The physical origin of Microsoft’s signals, including whether they reflect the required protected quantum phase, remains disputed.
A material route to the higher operating temperature and quantitative targets for its protective gap remain unresolved.
The decisive tests, acceptable error limits and criteria for judging protection still need definition.

page.title: Non-Abelian quantum operations at liquid-nitrogen temperature or above
page.definition: A solid-state material supports non-Abelian quasiparticles, collective excitations whose exchanges act in an order-dependent way, and fusion or braiding operations at or above nitrogen’s normal boiling point, approximately 77.34 K. An excitation gap and measured suppression of local-noise errors establish protection by the material’s topology.

goal.need: Microsoft’s Majorana roadmap cites electron thermometry of 50 mK; nitrogen’s normal boiling point is approximately 77.34 K, about 1,550 times higher. The roadmap links suppression of physical errors to the dimensionless ratios below. The goal is to retain non-Abelian operations and their protection at the higher material temperature.

figures.caption: A design example in Microsoft’s Majorana roadmap.
figures.note: These are design estimates, not measured gate errors. The roadmap also requires filtering, shielding and sufficient readout signal-to-noise ratio.

completion.title: Non-Abelian operations exhibit topological protection at nitrogen’s normal boiling point or above.
completion.criterion: At an active-material temperature at or above nitrogen’s normal boiling point at 101.325 kPa, approximately 77.34 K, demonstrate a gapped non-Abelian phase, its predicted fusion or braid transformations, and topological protection. The protection test is exponential suppression of identified local-noise errors as a published protection parameter increases, such as quasiparticle separation/coherence length or excitation gap/thermal energy. All three findings must concern the same material platform at the qualifying temperature.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback. The cited bodies establish topological-qubit and error-suppression objectives, but none establishes this combined temperature-specific test.
completion.basis: Searched NSF’s topological-qubit call, Microsoft’s device roadmaps, the SuperQuMap roadmap and high-temperature Majorana proposals; no outside completion test combined nitrogen-temperature operation with measured non-Abelian protection. This fallback joins the published qubit and error-suppression objectives to nitrogen’s normal boiling point. NIST supplies a material property, not a quantum-device performance standard.

milestones.title: A solid-state device reads a candidate fusion-channel label in a single shot.
milestones.criterion: Resolve in one measurement the charge or fermion-parity label used by a fusion protocol. Parity is an even or odd electron count. The paper published on 19 February 2025 studied two InAs–Al devices and reported 1% optimal assignment error, without unique topological identification. Microsoft’s preprint of 2 June 2026 reports approximately 20 s parity switching in one InAs–Pb nanowire; it is not peer reviewed. Legg disputed the earlier gap interpretation; Microsoft defended it in the comment and reply published on 24 June 2026.
milestones.set_by: Microsoft Azure Quantum’s published parity-readout protocol, written for superconducting nanowires. Klocke et al. describe the corresponding topological-charge readout requirement for spin-liquid qubits.
milestones.threshold_quote: allows determination of the parity in a single shot.

milestones.title: A solid-state device demonstrates non-Abelian fusion statistics against a deterministic control.
milestones.criterion: Measure fusion outcomes against the phase’s fusion rules and a control sequence. For Majorana modes, cross-pair fusion gives even and odd parity with probability 1/2 each; re-fusing original pairs is deterministic. Bilayer-graphene interference reported on 7 January 2026 covered two even-denominator states; its 2Φ₀ period at fixed filling did not identify non-Abelian statistics.
milestones.set_by: Aasen et al., Milestones Toward Majorana-Based Quantum Computing, Section III. The numerical probabilities were published for Majorana modes in superconducting islands; other cases require their phase-specific fusion rules.
milestones.threshold_quote: even and odd electron numbers for a given island with equal probability.

milestones.title: A solid-state device enacts a non-Abelian qubit transformation by braiding or fusion measurements.
milestones.criterion: Implement the phase’s braid matrix physically or through equivalent fusion measurements. In the Majorana protocol, one exchange of an initialized |0⟩ qubit gives equal |0⟩/|1⟩ probabilities; two exchanges give |1⟩ deterministically. Spin-liquid qubit initialization and gates are theoretical proposals in the cited paper. A 54-qubit trapped-ion demonstration realizes fusion and braiding on a processor, outside the solid-state material classes tracked here.
milestones.set_by: Aasen et al., Section V and Figure 11, written for Majorana nanowires; Microsoft Quantum’s measurement-based braid protocols; Klocke et al.’s spin-liquid protocols.
milestones.threshold_quote: demonstration of non-Abelian statistics by braiding in a branched geometry.

milestones.title: A solid-state device performs non-Abelian operations at nitrogen’s normal boiling point or above.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate the phase-specific fusion statistics or qubit transformations of the preceding protocols while the active material is at or above nitrogen’s normal boiling point at 101.325 kPa, approximately 77.34 K. Establish the non-Abelian phase and its excitation gap at that operating temperature. This precursor establishes elevated-temperature non-Abelian operations; the completion test additionally requires measured topological protection.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback. No temperature-specific experimental milestone was found in the cited roadmaps. NIST supplies only the normal boiling point.

not_found: No outside body was found to define a nitrogen-temperature completion test or its immediate precursor for protected non-Abelian operations.
No experiment meeting the elevated-temperature precursor or completion test was located for any of the three material platforms.
No common numerical confidence level or operation-error cutoff was found for certifying this elevated-temperature capability.
The complete published comment and reply of 24 June 2026 were unavailable beyond subscription previews.
